cards.q: Why is an outbound allowlist harder than an inbound one for modern applications?
cards.a: Because dependencies resolve to changing sets of addresses behind CDNs and cloud providers. Allowlisting by IP breaks constantly, so egress control usually needs a proxy that can filter by hostname instead.

cards.q: What is a NAT gateway in cloud terms and why does it exist?
cards.a: A managed device that lets instances in a private subnet make outbound connections without being reachable inbound. It is Node 9's NAT sold as a service, and it is a common surprise line item on a cloud bill.

cards.q: What is a bastion or jump host?
cards.a: A single hardened machine that is reachable from outside, through which you reach machines that are not. It shrinks the exposed surface to one auditable entry point.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic order, and why that order?
cards.a: Name, then route, then port, then TLS, then application — because each layer depends on the ones below it, so the first failure you find is the one worth fixing. Guessing which layer is broken is the most expensive mistake in this domain.

cards.q: What does dig tell you?
cards.a: The answer for a name, which record types exist, the TTL remaining, and which server answered. dig +trace walks the delegation from the root, bypassing your resolver's cache.

cards.q: How does traceroute actually work?
cards.a: It sends packets with TTL 1, then 2, then 3. Each successive router decrements the TTL to zero, discards the packet and reports back — so the replies reveal the path hop by hop. It is an elegant abuse of the loop-prevention mechanism.

cards.q: What does mtr add over traceroute?
cards.a: It runs continuously and shows per-hop loss and latency statistics over time, which distinguishes a hop that is genuinely dropping traffic from one that merely deprioritises replying to probes.

cards.q: Why can a middle hop in traceroute show 100% loss while the destination is fine?
cards.a: Because many routers rate-limit or refuse to generate ICMP replies for themselves while forwarding traffic perfectly. Loss at an intermediate hop only matters if it also appears at every hop after it.

cards.q: How do you test whether a TCP port is open, and nothing else?
cards.a: nc -vz host 443, or telnet host 443. It attempts a connection and stops, which cleanly separates a transport or firewall problem from an application problem.

cards.q: What does openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host show you?
cards.a: The certificate chain, the negotiated TLS version and cipher, and any validation error. The -servername flag is SNI — omit it on a multi-tenant host and you get the wrong certificate and a very confusing error.

cards.q: Why is curl -v the highest-value tool on the list?
cards.a: It prints the full request and response including headers, plus the DNS, connection and TLS steps as it does them. Most HTTP problems are visible in that output without any further tooling.

cards.q: What does curl -w give you and when is it the right first move?
cards.a: A timing breakdown — DNS lookup, TCP connect, TLS handshake, time to first byte, total. It is the right first move for any 'why is this slow' question, because it tells you which node of the stack the time is in.

cards.q: What does ss -tulpn answer?
cards.a: Which sockets are listening, on which addresses and ports, owned by which process. It answers 'is my server actually bound, and to loopback or all interfaces' and 'what is already using this port'.

cards.q: How would you count sockets stuck in TIME_WAIT?
cards.a: ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l. Useful when investigating whether ephemeral port exhaustion is plausible on a busy client.

cards.q: When do you escalate to tcpdump or Wireshark?
cards.a: When the other tools disagree or when you need ground truth — specifically, to prove whether a packet left the machine at all, or what exactly a peer sent before it reset the connection.

cards.q: A request is slow. What do you refuse to do before getting the timing breakdown?
cards.a: Form a hypothesis. Slow DNS, slow connect, slow TLS and slow application all feel identical from the outside and have entirely different fixes.

cards.q: What is the first question to ask about any connectivity failure?
cards.a: Whether it ever worked, and what changed. A failure that was always broken points at configuration; a failure that started points at a deploy, a certificate expiry, a DNS change or a scaling event.

cards.q: How do you tell a DNS problem from a connectivity problem in one step?
cards.a: Resolve the name, then connect directly to the resulting address. If the address works and the name does not, it is DNS; if neither works, it is below DNS.

cards.q: What does it mean when a service is reachable from one machine and not another?
cards.a: Almost always policy or path, not the service: a firewall or security group rule, a different DNS resolver, a proxy environment variable set in one place, or one machine being inside a private network the other is not.

cards.q: Why is intermittent failure often a load balancer problem?
cards.a: Because a request only fails when it lands on the one unhealthy backend. Consistent failure points at the whole service; a stable failure fraction points at one instance out of N.

cards.q: What does a container get, network-wise?
cards.a: Its own isolated network stack: its own interfaces, its own IP address, its own routing table, and its own view of which ports are in use.

cards.q: Why can two containers on one host both bind port 3000?
cards.a: Because those are two separate network stacks. The port number is only unique within a stack, and neither container is aware of the other's ports.

cards.q: A Docker bridge network is which earlier concept, in software?
cards.a: A switch — Node 2. It forwards frames between attached container interfaces and the host, learning where each address lives, exactly as a physical switch does.

cards.q: How do containers reach the internet?
cards.a: The host performs NAT on their behalf, rewriting the container's private source address to the host's address — Node 9's mechanism, implemented by the container runtime.

cards.q: What does -p 8080:3000 actually install?
cards.a: A NAT rule mapping the host's port 8080 to port 3000 inside the container. Without it the container is unreachable from outside, for exactly the reasons NAT makes any private machine unreachable.

cards.q: A container binds 127.0.0.1:3000 and the port is published. Why is it still unreachable?
cards.a: Because loopback inside the container's own network stack is not the host's loopback and not the bridge interface. The NAT rule forwards to the container's bridge address, where nothing is listening. Bind 0.0.0.0 instead.

cards.q: How do containers on a user-defined network reach each other by name?
cards.a: Docker runs an internal DNS server that resolves container and service names to their current addresses. It is Node 10's mechanism, scoped to that network.

cards.q: Why can an app in one container not reach a database at localhost:5432?
cards.a: Because localhost inside a container means that container. The database is a different network stack entirely, so you address it by service name — postgres:5432 — on the shared network.

cards.q: What is a Kubernetes Service, in terms of concepts you already have?
cards.a: A stable virtual name and address in front of a changing set of pods — a load balancer from Node 13 plus DNS from Node 10, so callers never need to know pod addresses.

cards.q: What is an Ingress?
cards.a: An L7 reverse proxy routing external traffic into the cluster by host and path — Node 13's reverse proxy, expressed as cluster configuration.

cards.q: What is a Kubernetes network policy?
cards.a: Firewall rules between pods — Node 16, scoped to the cluster. Without any policy the default is usually that every pod can reach every other pod.

cards.q: Why does container networking feel impenetrable to some people and straightforward to others?
cards.a: Because it contains nothing new. It is the switch, private addressing, NAT, DNS, load balancing and firewalling from earlier nodes, reimplemented in software. Anyone who never learned the physical version has to learn all of it at once, in disguise.

cards.q: What is host networking mode and when would you use it?
cards.a: The container shares the host's network stack directly — no isolation, no NAT, no port publishing, and port conflicts with the host become possible again. It is used for performance-sensitive or network-inspecting workloads and avoided otherwise.

cards.q: What is an overlay network?
cards.a: A virtual network spanning multiple hosts, where container traffic is encapsulated inside packets between the hosts. It lets containers on different machines behave as if they were on one flat network, at the cost of encapsulation overhead and a smaller effective MTU.

cards.q: Why do overlay networks make MTU problems more likely?
cards.a: Because encapsulation adds header bytes, so the usable payload is smaller than the underlying link's 1500. If that is not configured consistently, large packets get dropped and you see the classic small-requests-work signature.

cards.q: What is service discovery, and which two earlier nodes does it combine?
cards.a: The mechanism by which a caller finds the current address of a service that moves. It is naming from Node 10 plus health-aware selection from Node 13, and every orchestrator provides some version of it.

cards.q: What does host.docker.internal exist for?
cards.a: Reaching a service running on the host machine from inside a container, since localhost means the container. It is a convenience name provided by Docker Desktop rather than a general Linux feature.
